metadata.title: Skills on the Move: Migrants in the Survey of Adult Skills

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD report uses microdata from the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC) to compare assessed adult skills (literacy, numeracy, and problem solving) and their associations with labour-market and non-labour-market outcomes for migrants versus native-born adults. The excerpt provided does not specify whether OECD applied student/sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures in the reported estimates, so the weighting implementation cannot be confirmed from the text shown. For analysts working with PIAAC microdata, complex survey weights are typically required to produce population-representative estimates and to account for the multistage sampling design; therefore, users should apply the official PIAAC sampling weights and, where available, replicate weights for variance estimation. Because the provided text does not document the exact weight variable names or variance method, this extraction leaves weight usage as unverified rather than assuming a specific implementation.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report analyzes migrants’ skills and integration outcomes using the OECD Survey of Adult Skills (PIAAC). It documents that, on average across participating countries, foreign-born adults have lower assessed literacy, numeracy, and problem-solving proficiency than native-born adults, with large cross-country variation (e.g., gaps exceeding 50 points in Sweden and Finland, but under 8 points in Australia, the Czech Republic, Ireland, New Zealand, and Singapore). The report emphasizes within-country heterogeneity: migrant skill gaps vary by education level, where education was obtained, age at arrival, and duration of residence. A central mechanism highlighted is language disadvantage: the literacy gap between migrants and natives is much smaller when test-takers complete the assessment in their native language, and language penalties persist regardless of length of stay. The report further links skills to labour-market and non-labour-market outcomes, noting lower employment and earnings returns to education among migrants, and smaller differences in several well-being indicators such as self-reported health, alongside differences in trust and political efficacy in some countries.
